recordings.text: One piece, two victims. This is a fork: a single piece goes after several targets, and one move may not be enough to save them all.
Simple problem: this lets one of their pieces fork several targets. Before moving, look for the square where that piece could land.
Simple point: a fork was sitting right here, with one piece able to hit several targets, and the move played walks past it.
The main thing is the pin. That piece has its own king behind it on that line, so it cannot leave the line, and it stays stuck.
Simple problem: a pin against the king is now on offer for the other side, and a piece caught in it stays stuck in place.
A pin against the king was the better move, because it would have nailed a piece to its line. Here that piece gets to move freely.
Big idea: a skewer. The front piece is hit, it has to get out of the way, and the piece behind it is left to be taken.
Two pieces are lined up on one line, and now a skewer is on for the other side. When the front piece shifts off, the back piece is a target.
A skewer was the better move: the front piece is hit, it steps away, and the one behind is left to be taken. So that chance is gone.
The guard goes first. This move hits the defender, and whatever it was holding up is left with no help.
One defender is holding things together, and now the other side gets to knock it out. Look at what that defender holds up before it is gone.
The better move went after the defender. Without it, the piece it guarded would have stood with no help. As played, that defender is still standing guard.
Plain fact: its own pieces leave the king no air on the back row, and this move goes straight for it. That is mate on the back row in the making.
Simple problem: the king has no air. Its own pieces box it in on the back row, and the other side can aim for mate there.
The king was boxed in on its back row by its own pieces, so a back-rank mate was ready to go. The move played does something else.
The big thing is the pawn. It is walking toward the last row, where it gets promoted, so follow that walk.
One of their pawns now has a clear walk toward the last row, and if it gets there it is promoted. That pawn needs watching.
The better move cleared a pawn's walk to the last row and a promotion. The move played leaves that pawn sitting still.
The front piece clears out and a hidden attacker behind it comes alive. Big idea: a discovered attack, where moving one piece wakes up another.
Their front piece is standing in the way of a piece behind it, and this move lets it step aside so the back one can attack. Discovered attacks begin exactly like this.
There was a discovered attack in the better move. Clear the blocker away, and the back piece attacks as well. Not played here.
A single move, aimed at two things. That is a double attack, and the defense has to deal with both of them.
With this, the other side gets a double attack. Any reply has to cover both targets.
Two at once: that is what the better move hit. A double attack was there, and the move played makes no such threat.
This move drags a defender off its post, so whatever it was guarding has no cover now. Plain deflection.
A single defender carries a lot here, and the other side can now drag it away and leave that work undone. Deflection is the name for that.
Dragging a defender off its post was the better move. That chance to deflect it is left on the board.
Simple point: it was loose, and this move takes it.
The better move takes a piece with no guard on it. The move played leaves it sitting there. Loose pieces come first.
Simple problem: one piece has nobody guarding it, so the other side gets it for nothing.
Simple problem: this moves the only real defender away from a piece. That piece can now be collected.
With its last move, the opponent made a threat, and this move does nothing about it; a piece hangs because of it. The other side's move always gets looked at first.
This capture starts a bad trade. The recapture takes back a bigger piece. Count a trade all the way to its last capture.
Bottom line: a minor piece is out of its starting spot and ready to work.
Development was there with a different move.
Big plus for the rook: the file it stands on has no pawns of either color, so it has a clear road.
A different move would have put a rook on a file empty of pawns.
Big change for this rook: its file is half open now. Its own pawns are gone from it, and an enemy pawn still sits up ahead.
A different move would have set a rook on a half-open file, its own pawns gone and an enemy pawn still there to aim at.
Big thing: a passed pawn. No enemy pawn waits ahead to stop it, on its own file or either side file.
Another move would have turned a pawn into a passer, its own file and both side files clear of enemy pawns ahead.
Up goes the passed pawn, a row closer to promotion. It was free already; now it has less distance left.
With a different move, the passer would have gone up one more row.
Big picture: no friendly pawn is near this one any more. With no friendly pawn on the files beside it, no pawn can help guard it.
A different move would have left a pawn standing by itself with no friendly pawn next door on either side.
Simple point: a loose piece now has protection. It is not hanging any more.
A different move would have given cover to a loose piece.
Plain fact: this piece has lost its guard. Weak spot, yes; lost piece, no.
Another move would have taken the last guard away from a piece. A loose piece is a target, not a lost piece.
Simple point: the king gets elbow room, one more legal square. Good to have that room.
A different move would have given the king more breathing room.
Castling: the king tucks away to the side, and the rook comes over next to it, all in a single move.
Castling was there instead, king tucked away and rook brought out on the same move.
After this capture, that side's two bishops are not a pair any more. That side is left without one bishop for the light squares and one for the dark.
With a different move, a bishop capture would have broken up the opponent's pair.
Bottom line: doubled pawns. That side has two pawns on a single file now, stacked up, and neither can guard the other.
Doubled pawns would have come from a different move, two pawns of one color stacked up.
This is the big problem: from this point, mate by force belongs to the other side. Track back to where the defense broke.
Big picture: mate by force was there, and the move played skips it. When the king is trapped, look at every check first.
Material goes, and the idea holds. If the material is grabbed, the checked line still works. That is strong.
Simple point: anything else that was checked goes down. This was the one move left standing. Good defense.
Plain fact: no other checked move kept the edge. With anything else, the advantage was gone.
Simple problem: something is loose, and the reply takes it at once. Look at the reply and find the loose piece.
Check is the best answer. When the king is attacked, that is the first thing to deal with.
The engine has a different move on top. Play that one as well, then see how the replies differ.
The engine has a better move than this one. The cost shows up in the reply.
Strong. Out of everything the engine weighed, this move gives up next to nothing.
This is sound. The engine likes another move more, but the value of the position mostly stays.
Simple point: this one is straight out of opening theory. A known line is one thing. Understanding the position is another.
This is the move where known opening theory runs out. From now on, the players are working it out for themselves.
The earlier setback is fixed; this move gets the game back on track. Good. Keep building from here.
Some of the other side's mistakes helped, and the game is playable again after the earlier setback. Take that, but do not count on it.
The opponent made a slip on the last move, and this move cashes in. Good.
The opponent just blundered, and nobody makes them pay here. When they slip, look for the punishment.
Bottom line: this game has run into the same problem once already. Lay the two moments next to each other and find the common thread.
Big picture: the earlier loose piece is safe behind a guard now. Good.
Not one big mistake. A few small slips have added up, and this move is one more of those.
The advantage was kept, move after move, until the game was won. That is how to finish.
Simple point: the saved games have this problem in them more than once. That makes it worth real study.
Checkmate. Nowhere left for that king to go. Finished.
Checkmate. That king has no move left. The defense broke earlier, so go back and find that spot.
A draw. The result is settled, but the moves are still worth a look.
Look at the board, then pick a move.
Not quite. Back to the board; a different move this time.
That try did not get checked. Go back to the move and play it again.
Saved engine analysis: the side that played this move has a forced mate in hand.
Saved engine analysis: after this move, mate is forced against the side that played it.
At the last move of the saved line, count the material. The side that played this move has more than it had at the start.
At the last move of the saved line, count the material. The side that played this move has less than it had at the start.
This exercise takes the move as correct. No clear tactical reason here, and no made-up one either.
Wrong answer for this exercise. There is no clear tactical reason in these moves either way.
Plain fact: the exercise lists this move among its saved answers. In this exercise, that list is the rule.
Simple point: the exercise did not save this move as an answer. It is not bad chess for that. This exercise simply wants something else.
Look at this move until it makes sense. Then move on.
Good move. Hold on to the why, too.
Practice saved, and the schedule for review is untouched.
Solved. This recall still stays on the relearning list for now.
Start here, with the position before any of the moves we look at.
Next move. See what changed.
Check. The king is under attack, and that comes before everything.
This move ends the check on the king.
Up to the last row, and the pawn is promoted.
Up to the last row, and the pawn is promoted with check.
Up to the last row, and the pawn is promoted. That is checkmate, and the king is trapped.
The pawn makes it to the last row and is promoted, and that same move gets its king out of check.
A capture.
Capture and check together. The piece takes, and the king is attacked.
Something is captured, and it is checkmate. The king cannot get away.
A capture, and the capture is what gets the king out of check.
One pawn move does it all: a capture, and a promotion on the last row.
The pawn captures as it reaches the last row, is promoted, and gives check.
One pawn move does it all: a capture, and a promotion on the last row. Checkmate follows, with the king trapped.
One pawn move does it all: a capture, and a promotion on the last row. That same move lifts the check on its king.
The king castles, and the rook gives check from its new square.
Castling ends the game with checkmate. The enemy king is caught with no way out.
Here the fork collects. One piece goes after several targets, takes one, and this example comes out ahead in material.
Pinned to its king, that piece may not make the capture shown, because stepping off the line would give the king away.
The attacked piece has its king behind it, so it is pinned. Its only moves are ones that still cover the king, so running is hard.
Not one defender may take back, because each of them is pinned to its king. That makes the capture work, and material is won in the line shown.
With its king behind it, the pinned piece is nailed to that line. As these moves go on, it gets taken.
Bottom line: once the front piece is gone from the line, whatever was behind it is captured.
Check. The king must move out of the way. Then the same attacker wins what was behind the king.
First the guard goes, and it was the only guard. The piece it was protecting falls later in these moves.
First the defender gets dragged away, then the piece it was protecting gets taken.
Front piece moves, the line clears, and the back piece makes a capture along it.
Move the front piece, and check comes from behind it.
Two checks land on the king in the same move: double check. Nothing but a king move will do against that.
One piece moves and attacks, and the line it leaves lets a second attacker in. Here, that second attacker takes what it was aiming at.
The pawn is promoted, and in this example that side ends the line with extra material.
That piece was loose, so it goes. This example ends with the capturing side holding extra material.
Big picture: the attacking piece was under a relative pin, and the opponent's last move freed it. The target did not move, so in the line shown it is taken.
Nothing in the rules stops the other side from playing that marked move. Try that reply on the board and judge what follows.
Before every move, find any piece of yours that could be taken for nothing.
Loose enemy pieces get checked before any quiet move.
Go through every forcing move hunting for a fork on two valuable targets.
Before moving a pinned piece, look past it down the line: the king may be there, or a bigger piece.
An attack can go straight through the first piece. Look for a valuable piece lined up behind it.
A defender about to be traded: see what it guards first.
A blocker that moves opens up whatever line is behind it. Follow it to the end.
Some moves carry two threats at once. Look hard for those. Checks and opened lines both count as threats.
A back-row defender leaving means the king may lose its air. Check for an escape square first.
Count the pawn's moves to promotion, and look at every forcing pawn push.
A defender about to move: first count what it guards. All of that loses its guard when it leaves.
A trade gets counted to the very end, every capture on both sides.
A forcing trade may drag a defender away from a second job it has. Watch for it.
This one is measured against the saved answers. Moves outside that list may still be fine chess.
The replies in these moves are strong ones. A strong reply is not always the only reply.
Only the line shown is counted for material, starting where it starts. Piece values for that count are in the written notes.
No single simple tactic explains the saved line. Run through it move by move and compare how the replies differ. No positional reason is assumed either.
The saved answer setting decides this explanation. Which one is set is in the written notes.
Here comes your study line, move by move.
Right. It belongs to the line you are learning.
The answer is somewhere in your picked study lines. One of those moves fits here.
Several moves from your picked opening lines are fine here. Any of them counts.
Only one move here comes from your study material. Find it.
Not in the opening lines you picked. Try again.
Not one of your picked opening moves. Try again. The study was changed, and its review dates stay where they are.
Not one of your picked opening moves. Try again. Because this position is retired, nothing about its schedule moves.
Any move in this line is good enough for mixed Due. Dedicated practice sticks to this single line.
The recall schedule tests the side you picked. One card covers a position that several active studies share.
Simple fix: the session has to be reloaded before the next move.
Here the board runs the checked line.
Answer shown, and this try is saved that way. Play it through below.
Second try, and solved. Both go on your record: the miss, then the finish.
Not one wrong move from start to finish. Good.
Not the puzzle's move. Moves played right before it are kept.
Right move. The puzzle is not done yet. Another move is waiting.
No rush. Think it through, then move.
Not enough from the engine on this one, so I have no explanation to give.
Review on pause. Start it again below, or push a piece around to look.
Pick a move to review it, or try a move of your own.
Simple point: book move.
Plain fact: this is a move theory has seen many times.
Book. Theory has written this one down.
Still book.
Book again for this one.
Both sides are still in theory with the reply.
Known line, still going.
More book.
The book again, one more time.
Still covered by the opening books.
Book again. Book does not mean good.
This is the beginning. Go forward, and we'll look at the big ideas.
That one is not what this chapter teaches. Check the board and pick a new one.
Right move. That is the one the chapter wants.
Answer shown on the board. Look at it, then go on.
Now the moves play by themselves. Just watch them go.
Your turn. Remember the move you studied here.
Different idea here. The main path still waits.
Chapter done. Progress kept safe.
All of the game is here now. Look around, then go back to the chapter.
Simple fix: press reload, then carry on.
